common_name: Vardar Valley Boxwood (Low Broad Flat-Topped Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Vardar Valley is a low, broad boxwood selected from seed collected in Macedonia for exceptional heat and cold tolerance.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade with some direct sun. Vardar Valley grows into a distinctive low, broad, flat-topped mound with dark blue-green foliage, wider than it is tall, making it a good choice for a low, informal hedge or foundation planting where a rounded ball shape isn't wanted. Selected from wild seed collected in the Balkans, it shows notably good tolerance of both summer heat and winter cold compared to many other boxwood cultivars. It grows slowly and holds its shape well with only light annual shearing.

common_name: Elegantissima Boxwood (Cream-Margined Variegated Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Elegantissima is a variegated boxwood cultivar grown for its cream-edged foliage.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade with some direct sun, which helps preserve the variegation better than deep shade. Elegantissima bears small, rounded leaves narrowly edged in creamy white, giving the whole shrub a soft, luminous appearance quite different from the solid green of most boxwood, and it holds this variegation year-round on a compact, rounded shrub. It grows a bit slower than solid-green boxwood cultivars and is a good choice for adding brightness to a shady foundation planting or mixed border. Shear lightly once or twice a season to maintain a tidy form.

common_name: Justin Brouwers Boxwood (Small Dense Compact Rounded Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Justin Brouwers stays naturally small and dense, needing little pruning to hold its shape.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade with some direct sun. Justin Brouwers forms a naturally dense, tidy, rounded mound of small, dark green leaves without heavy shearing, staying compact for many years and making it a low-maintenance choice for edging, small hedges, or foundation plantings where a naturally neat form is wanted. Its small mature size suits it to tight spaces where larger boxwood cultivars would quickly outgrow the site. Light shearing once a year keeps the form especially crisp, but is not strictly necessary.

common_name: Green Beauty Boxwood (Heat-Tolerant Dark-Green Rounded Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Green Beauty holds its deep green color through winter better than many boxwood cultivars, which tend to bronze in cold weather.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Green Beauty forms a dense, rounded shrub of rich, glossy dark green foliage that resists the bronzing common in many boxwood cultivars through winter cold, staying attractive year-round. It also tolerates summer heat and humidity better than English boxwood, making it a reliable, low-fuss choice for hedges and foundation plantings across a wide range of Southern climates. Shear once or twice a season to maintain a tidy form, and prune to allow good air circulation through the interior to reduce disease pressure.

common_name: Sherwoodii Abelia (Fine-Textured Dense Compact Abelia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Sherwoodii is a fine-textured, dense, compact abelia selection that rarely sets flowers, grown mainly for its neat foliage form.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Sherwoodii forms an unusually dense, fine-textured mound of small, glossy leaves, arching gracefully like other glossy abelia cultivars but staying more compact and tidy, and flowering only sparsely compared to typical abelia, making it valued primarily as a refined foliage shrub rather than for bloom. Its neat, rounded habit suits low hedges, foundation plantings, and mixed borders where a fine texture is wanted without the arching sprawl of larger abelia selections. It tolerates heat and drought well once established and needs only light pruning to maintain shape.

common_name: Compacta Abelia (Dwarf Dense Rounded Pink-White Abelia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Compacta is a dwarf glossy abelia selection well suited to smaller foundation plantings.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Compacta forms a dense, rounded shrub noticeably smaller than the straight species, bearing clusters of small, fragrant, funnel-shaped pink-and-white flowers from summer into fall on arching branches. Its manageable size fits foundation plantings and smaller borders better than full-size glossy abelia, while still drawing bees and butterflies through its long bloom season. It tolerates heat and drought well once established and needs only light pruning after the main flush to maintain shape.

common_name: Little Richard Abelia (Compact White-Flowered Rebloomer)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Richard is a compact, heavy-blooming white-flowered abelia selection.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Little Richard forms a rounded, compact shrub bearing abundant clusters of fragrant white flowers from late spring into fall, blooming more heavily and over a longer season than many other compact abelia selections. Its manageable size and long bloom period make it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for a foundation planting or low hedge that draws pollinators for months. It tolerates heat and drought well once established and needs only light pruning to maintain shape.

common_name: Golden Anniversary Abelia (Gold-and-Green Variegated Abelia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Golden Anniversary bears gold-and-green variegated foliage that turns purple-red in fall.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, which brings out the brightest gold variegation. Golden Anniversary bears leaves brightly marked in gold and green that shift to purple-red tones in fall, giving the shrub multi-season foliage interest beyond its clusters of small white summer flowers. Its bold variegation makes it a strong accent in a mixed border, especially paired with dark-foliaged companions for contrast. It tolerates heat and drought well once established and needs only light pruning after the main bloom flush to maintain shape.

common_name: Blush Loropetalum (Dwarf Soft Pink Chinese Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Blush is a dwarf loropetalum selection with soft pink flowers and green-tinged burgundy foliage.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Blush forms a dense, compact mound bearing soft, gentle pink, fringe-petaled flowers over foliage that leans more green than the deep burgundy typical of many loropetalum cultivars, giving it a softer overall look for gardens wanting a subtler color than the bold magenta-and-purple selections common in the trade. Its dwarf habit suits foundation plantings and low borders without the need for constant pruning to control size. Prune lightly right after the main spring bloom to shape, since later pruning removes developing flower buds.

common_name: Razzleberri Loropetalum (Dwarf Burgundy-Foliage Hot-Pink Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Razzleberri is a dwarf, mounding loropetalum selection with burgundy foliage and hot-pink flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, where the deepest foliage color develops. Razzleberri forms a dense, mounding shrub with rich burgundy-purple foliage held year-round and covered each spring in vivid hot-pink, fringe-petaled flowers, with foliage color holding better through summer heat than some older loropetalum selections. Its dwarf, mounded habit suits it to foundation plantings, low borders, and mass plantings without the need for constant pruning. Prune lightly right after the main spring bloom to shape, since later pruning removes developing flower buds.

common_name: Snow Panda Loropetalum (Green-Foliage White-Flowered Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Snow Panda is a green-foliage, white-flowered loropetalum selection with a compact mounding habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Snow Panda pairs clean green evergreen foliage with abundant white, fringe-petaled flowers in spring and scattered rebloom later in the season, a softer, more traditional look than the burgundy-leaved, pink-flowered loropetalum cultivars that dominate the trade. Its compact, mounding habit works well as a low hedge, foundation planting, or mixed-border companion to burgundy loropetalum for contrast. Prune lightly right after the main spring bloom to shape, since later pruning removes developing flower buds.

common_name: Black Pearl Loropetalum (Near-Black Foliage Hot-Pink Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Black Pearl is a compact loropetalum selection with some of the darkest foliage available in the species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun for the darkest foliage color. Black Pearl bears exceptionally dark, near-black purple foliage year-round, among the deepest coloring available in loropetalum, contrasted each spring by clusters of vivid hot-pink, fringe-petaled flowers. Its compact, dense habit works well as a dramatic accent, mixed border anchor, or low hedge where strong color contrast against green-leaved neighbors is wanted. Prune lightly right after the main spring bloom to shape, since later pruning removes developing flower buds.

common_name: Nana Purpurea Nandina (Dwarf Red-Purple Winter Foliage Heavenly Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Nana Purpurea is a dwarf, mounding nandina selection prized for red-purple winter foliage color.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade, where the strongest winter color develops. Nana Purpurea forms a dense, low mound of finely textured foliage that shifts from summer green to rich red-purple with the onset of cold weather, providing seasonal color in a shrub that never flowers or sets the invasive berries of the straight species. Its dwarf size suits it to low borders, foundation plantings, and mass plantings without pruning to control height. It tolerates heat and drought well once established and needs little routine care.

common_name: Alba Nandina (White-Berried Light-Green Heavenly Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba is an unusual white-berried nandina selection with lighter green foliage than the species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Alba bears the same upright, cane-like habit and airy, compound foliage typical of nandina, but with lighter green summer color that turns bronze rather than red in cold weather, and clusters of unusual creamy-white berries in fall and winter that persist well into the following spring, a striking departure from the familiar red-berried species. Its upright canes and winter berry display make it a good architectural accent or informal screen. Prune out the oldest canes at ground level occasionally to keep the clump renewing itself with fresh growth.

common_name: Filamentosa Nandina (Fine Thread-Leaf Heavenly Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Filamentosa is a fine-textured nandina selection with unusually narrow, thread-like leaflets.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade, where the best orange-red fall and winter color develops. Filamentosa bears unusually narrow, thread-fine leaflets that give the entire shrub a soft, lacy, almost fern-like texture very different from the broader-leaved standard nandina, turning warm orange-red in cold weather. Its fine texture makes an interesting contrast planting alongside bolder-leaved shrubs and perennials. It tolerates heat and drought well once established and needs little routine care beyond occasional thinning of old canes.

common_name: Wood's Dwarf Nandina (Very Compact Fiery Winter-Color Heavenly Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Wood's Dwarf is one of the smallest nandina selections available, with intense fiery winter foliage color.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade, where the most intense winter color develops. Wood's Dwarf is among the most compact nandina selections in the trade, forming a dense, tidy mound that turns a vivid fiery red-orange in cold weather, providing dramatic seasonal color in a footprint small enough for tight foundation plantings or containers. Like other dwarf nandina cultivars it never flowers or sets the invasive berries of the straight species. It tolerates heat and drought well once established and needs little routine care.

common_name: Royal Princess Nandina (Lacy Blue-Green Open-Habit Heavenly Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Royal Princess bears finely divided, lacy blue-green foliage on an open, upright habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Royal Princess bears finely divided, lacy, blue-green foliage on an open, airy, upright habit, a refined texture and color quite different from the coarser, denser look of standard nandina, softened further by clusters of white flowers and red berries. Its open habit and cool foliage color pair well with fine-textured ferns and grasses in a mixed shade border. Prune out the oldest canes at ground level occasionally to keep the clump renewing itself with fresh growth.

common_name: Miami Supreme Gardenia (Heat-Tolerant Large Double White Gardenia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in partial shade; Miami Supreme was bred specifically for reliable flowering under the intense heat and humidity of the Deep South and Florida.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Miami Supreme bears large, fully double, intensely fragrant white flowers on a vigorous, upright shrub bred specifically to hold up to the extreme heat and humidity of the Deep South and Florida, where some gardenia cultivars struggle to set or hold buds. Its bold flower size and dependable performance under tough summer conditions have made it a favorite for Gulf Coast gardens. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer through the growing season, keep soil consistently moist, and prune right after the main spring-into-summer bloom to shape.

common_name: Belmont Gardenia (Vigorous Large Double White Gardenia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in partial shade; Belmont is a vigorous, upright gardenia selection bearing large, fully double, fragrant flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Belmont grows into one of the larger, more vigorous gardenia cultivars, producing large, fully double, intensely fragrant white flowers on an upright shrub well suited to use as a tall hedge, screen, or specimen where its eventual size can be accommodated. Its vigor and heavy bloom make it a reliable choice for gardeners wanting a substantial, floriferous gardenia rather than a compact form. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer through the growing season, keep soil consistently moist, and prune right after the main bloom flush to shape and control size.

common_name: George Lindley Taber Azalea (Light Pink Darker-Blotched Southern Indica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; George Lindley Taber is a large, vigorous Southern Indica azalea and parent to the popular white-flowered sport Mrs. G. G. Gerbing.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade under filtered light such as high pines or open hardwoods. George Lindley Taber bears large, light pink flowers with a darker pink blotch and edging, opening in a massive mid-spring flush on a big, vigorous Southern Indica shrub that can reach well over 8 feet with age, a scale typical of old Gulf South gardens where century-old specimens are still common. It is the parent plant behind the popular white-flowered sport Mrs. G. G. Gerbing, discovered as a branch mutation. Prune immediately after bloom, since flower buds set on the current season's growth and later pruning removes next year's flowers.

common_name: Mrs. G. G. Gerbing Azalea (Pure White Large-Flowered Southern Indica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Mrs. G. G. Gerbing is a white-flowered sport of George Lindley Taber, one of the most widely planted white azaleas in the South.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade under filtered light such as high pines or open hardwoods. A white-flowered sport of George Lindley Taber, Mrs. G. G. Gerbing bears large, pure white flowers in an overwhelming mid-spring flush that can blanket a mature shrub in solid white bloom, growing into a large, vigorous, long-lived specimen that anchors many older Gulf South gardens. Its clean white color makes it a classic pairing with pink and magenta Southern Indica azaleas for a layered spring display. Prune immediately after bloom, since flower buds set on the current season's growth and later pruning removes next year's flowers.

common_name: Hinodegiri Azalea (Classic Small Bright Red Kurume Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Hinodegiri is one of the original Kurume azalea cultivars introduced to the West in the early 20th century.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade under filtered light. Hinodegiri is one of the original Kurume azalea cultivars brought to the West from Japan in the early 20th century and remains a benchmark for the group, bearing masses of small, bright red flowers that all but cover the dense, compact, twiggy shrub in mid-spring. Its fine-textured foliage and tidy habit make it useful as a low hedge or foundation planting distinct from the larger, looser Southern Indica azaleas. Prune immediately after bloom, since flower buds set on the current season's growth and later pruning removes next year's flowers.

common_name: Gumpo Pink Azalea (Dwarf Low-Spreading Pink Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Gumpo Pink is a dwarf, late-blooming Satsuki azalea popular for bonsai and low borders.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade under filtered light. Gumpo Pink forms a very low, dense, spreading mound bearing large, soft pink flowers in late spring into early summer, blooming weeks after most other azalea groups have finished, which extends the azalea season in a Gulf South garden. Its low, ground-hugging habit makes it useful as an edging plant, rock garden specimen, or bonsai subject, distinct from the taller, more upright Kurume and Southern Indica types. Prune immediately after bloom, since flower buds set on the current season's growth and later pruning removes next year's flowers.

common_name: Wakaebisu Azalea (Salmon-Pink Satsuki Bonsai Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Wakaebisu is a classic Satsuki azalea especially popular as a bonsai subject in Japan.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade under filtered light. Wakaebisu bears salmon-pink flowers on a low, spreading Satsuki azalea prized in Japan as one of the classic cultivars for bonsai training, valued for its tolerance of the repeated root and branch pruning that bonsai technique requires as much as for its late-spring bloom. Grown as a garden shrub rather than trained as bonsai, it forms a dense, low mound similar to other Satsuki types, blooming weeks after Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas have finished. Prune immediately after bloom, since flower buds set on the current season's growth and later pruning removes next year's flowers.

common_name: Betty Anne Voss Azalea (Salmon-Pink Double Robin Hill Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Betty Anne Voss is a Robin Hill azalea prized for large, hose-in-hose double blooms and a spreading habit.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade under filtered light. Betty Anne Voss bears large, hose-in-hose double blooms in soft salmon-pink on a wide-spreading, low-mounding Robin Hill azalea, a breeding group developed for cold hardiness and large flower size on a more compact plant than Southern Indica types. Its spreading habit works well massed as a groundcover-like planting under high shade or as an underplanting for taller shrubs and trees. Prune immediately after bloom, since flower buds set on the current season's growth and later pruning removes next year's flowers.

common_name: Watchet Azalea (Large Pale Pink Dark-Blotched Robin Hill Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Watchet is a Robin Hill azalea with unusually large, dark-blotched pale pink flowers on a spreading habit.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade under filtered light. Watchet bears unusually large, pale pink flowers marked with a bold, dark blotch, opening on a low, wide-spreading Robin Hill azalea bred for large flower size on a compact, cold-hardy plant. Its spreading habit suits it to underplanting taller shrubs or massing as a flowering groundcover in dappled shade. Prune immediately after bloom, since flower buds set on the current season's growth and later pruning removes next year's flowers.
